Unable to cultivate superior supramundane merit, one cultivates only a superior intention (*āśaya*).
This exceptional resolve is not present in the old edition of the sutra.
[The Sutra says: "If one is in the Brahma-heaven... up to bringing benefit and happiness."
The commentary states:
These three phrases clarify that [the title] resides in the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
Brahmā dwells in the first dhyāna; it is said that he is uniquely honored throughout the world.
Now, the various distinctions among the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are shown so that it may be known they are not exclusively supreme.
Furthermore, as each of the four dhyānas can serve as a sovereign state, their specific differences have not yet been fixed.
The old commentary states: "He instructed him with superior wisdom, though he had not yet attained all the concentrations."
Śakra, while dwelling in heaven, often harbors the notion of permanence; [the Buddha] demonstrates to him that all sovereign powers are impermanent.
The Four World-Protecting Kings, each presiding over their respective regions, are commanded to protect all beings with impartial benefit and happiness.
Sūtra: This is Vimalakīrti’s arrival and his benefiting of sentient beings.
Commentary:
This is the second summary of former skillful means.
This skillfulness is entirely the wisdom of expedient means (*upāya-prajñā*).
Furthermore, it is called a "gate" because it can give rise to all merit and wisdom.
The Sūtra says: "By means of expedient means, he manifests himself as being ill."
The commentary states:
This is the second section below, which reveals his present provisional [teachings].
Within this, there are further two parts:
First is the skillful means of manifesting the body, because the body possesses illness.
Second is the skillful means of manifesting speech, because speech expounds the Dharma.
This refers to the skillful means of the body.
Question:
Since there are many kinds of skillful means for manifesting the body according to one's will, why does he now manifest his body as being ill?
Answer:
The purpose of manifesting illness is briefly of ten kinds: first, because those who come to inquire after one’s illness do so for the sake of transformation;

second, because it is hoped that the World-Honored One will cause [others] to inquire after one’s illness; third, to reveal that from time immemorial all bodies are subject to illness; fourth, to clarify that illness arises in accordance with the mind of compassion; fifth, to enable the recognition of the causes of illness among both ordinary beings and sages; sixth, to cause those who are ill to subdue their minds; seventh, to cause those of lower status to know that they are not of the same class; eighth, because only those of wondrous, detailed, and high virtue are able to respond appropriately; ninth, because engaging in dialogue serves as a great benefit; and tenth, to manifest the greatness of the Tathāgata’s physical majesty and virtue.
As shown in the following scriptural passage, it is not necessary to set it forth in full detail.
Scripture: "Because of his illness... up to "...all [the monks] were affected by his illness. Commentary:
The following section reveals the power of skillful means (*upāya*).
It contains two parts:
first, the clarification of those to be converted; second, the formal elucidation of skillful means itself.
This is the opening passage.
All those who inquire after his illness are beings to be converted.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, Vimalakīrti arrived and extensively expounded the Dharma for them."
The commentary states:
Below, the provisional [teachings] are correctly elucidated.
There are two parts:
First a brief indication, followed by a detailed exposition; this is that indication.
The Sūtra says: "O virtuous ones, [from birth] until one cannot rely on it."
The commentary states:
This reveals the provisional power of speech.
There are three [aspects]:
First, one is taught to cultivate weary detachment;
next, one is exhorted to aspire with joyful seeking. The passage below—"O virtuous ones!

You should give rise to weary detachment toward the body of the Tathāgata, and you should arouse joyful aspiration toward the body of the Tathāgata"—is an example of this, for all gates of practice do not exceed these two.
The subsequent section clarifies the benefits, beginning with: "This Vimalakīrti, for those who have come to the assembly to inquire after his illness, preaches the Dharma according to their needs.
This initial passage consists of five parts, as they teach the arising of five kinds of contemplations that lead to disillusionment and destruction [of worldly attachments].
First, contemplating the meaning of impermanence through the arising and ceasing [of phenomena];
second, from "afflicted by suffering" onwards, contemplating oppression, which is the meaning of suffering;
third, from "this body is like a mass of foam" onwards, contemplating that it is not substantially existent, which is the meaning of emptiness.
4. From "This body has no master" onwards, it praises its lack of autonomy; this is the meaning of *anātman* (non-self). 5.
From "This body is impure" onwards, it praises its susceptibility to defilement; this is the meaning of *aśubha* (impurity).

Regarding the method of entering meditative contemplation: one first contemplates impermanence; because it is impermanent, it is suffering; because it is suffering, it is empty; because it is empty, it is non-self; and thus one enters the True Truth (*satya*).
Now, by adding the contemplation of impurity, one causes a profound sense of revulsion to arise.
This praises the impermanence of arising and ceasing; since there is no such thing as eternal existence, for the eternal lacks any defining characteristic.
While it generally indicates impermanence, it also specifically reveals that "arising" is the root of impermanence, and thus receives the name "impermanence."

True Suchness (tathatā) is eternally existent, whereas the divine self (ātman) is eternally non-existent. This conditioned body was originally non-existent and now exists; its existence is not eternal, and thus it differs from True Suchness.
Originally existing and then returning to non-existence, its non-existence is not eternal non-existence, and thus it differs from the divine self.
Because there is no characteristic of permanence, it is said to be impermanent.
The remaining three characteristics are explained individually.
"Lacking strength" refers to the characteristic of aging and death, because they destroy the power of life-force.
The above collectively reveals that throughout the course of a single lifetime, all things are impermanent, decaying and fleeting, arising and ceasing from moment to moment.

One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*; sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*; thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*; eighteen *muhūrtas* constitute one *yāma*; twelve *yāmas* constitute one day; thirty days constitute one month; and twelve months constitute one year.
In this way, a single lifetime is cut into immeasurable births and deaths.
Alternatively, "impermanence" is the general term for this impermanence:
it possesses no powerful cessation, no firm momentum, and no robust strength; rather, it decays and returns to its source.
Because every thought-moment is swift and deceives and deludes people, it cannot be relied upon or trusted as being permanent.

Furthermore, the body in the desire realm lacks strength, the body in the form realm lacks solidity, and the body in the formless realm lacks power; all are decaying and swift, phenomena that cannot be relied upon for trust.
Sūtra: "Afflicted by suffering... [it is] a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay.
Commentary: This refers to contemplating the state of oppression from below.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the characteristics of suffering; second, the exhortation to rely upon oneself.
This is the initial section.
Suffering is so called because it is afflicted by the eight sufferings and the three types of suffering.
As for the eight sufferings: first is the suffering of birth, which has two aspects:
first, being oppressed by manifold sufferings; second, serving as the basis upon which other sufferings depend.
Within the mother’s womb, between the amnion and the chorion, one undergoes the oppression of various extremely impure substances;
at the very moment of emerging from the womb, one subsequently experiences the great suffering of the compression of the limbs and body.
Thereafter, various sufferings such as old age, illness, and death continue to follow in succession.
Second is the suffering of old age, because it is the suffering of the deterioration of one's temporal state.
Third is the suffering of illness, because it is the suffering of the transformation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Fourth is the suffering of death, because of the suffering arising from the transformation and decay of the life-span.
Fifth is the suffering of association with the hated, because of the suffering arising from such association.
Sixth is the suffering of separation from the beloved, because of the suffering arising from such separation.
Seventh is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, for the failure to achieve what is desired gives rise to suffering.
As a verse says:
"For those who pursue various desires, hopes and expectations constantly arise; if those desires are not fulfilled, the resulting distress and ruin are like being struck by an arrow."
Briefly summarized, all five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are suffering because they consist of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), instability, and the arising of suffering.

They are afflicted by these eight types of suffering; they serve as the vessel for the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*); they abound in various faults and calamities; they are pursued by one hundred and five kinds of suffering; they are phenomena subject to transformation and decay that do not endure for long; and because they are impermanent, they are suffering.
The impermanence of the arising aspect is suffering because it serves as a condition; its nature as suffering can be understood.
The impermanence of the cessation aspect is suffering because it involves disintegration; its nature as suffering can be understood.

Because all things are impermanent by nature, they are characterized as the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) due to their dependence on conditions; thus, their nature can be understood.
Therefore, the meaning of suffering is explained through the concept of transformation and decay.
Sūtra: "O worthy ones, [all conditioned phenomena] are not to be relied upon."
The commentary states:
This exhorts one not to rely [on anything].
Do not rely on this evil body to give rise to delusion and karma.
Because those known as wise people, who possess hearing-wisdom (*śrutaprajñā*), do not rely upon them, all who rely [upon such things] are deluded beings.
Sūtra: This body is like a collection of dharmas... arising from mere inversion.
The commentary states:
The following ten phrases observe that [phenomena] do not exist as real entities.
The real dharmas that are grasped have the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) as their nature; because they are not real, they are empty.

Regarding the five phrases herein, as for the body being "like a collection of dharmas," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (84) states: "Because it increases and decreases rapidly; because it is produced from the water element; because it is produced by the water of food and drink through the savoring of flavors; because it cannot be kneaded or squeezed; and because, unlike a lump of clay, it cannot be transformed or fashioned into other objects."
This sutra states that it "cannot be grasped or rubbed"; "grasping or rubbing" carries the sense of kneading or crushing.
Furthermore, while it is not actually an aggregate, it appears as one, and is thus able to give rise to understanding in sentient beings.
That which is like a floating bubble arises from the conjunction of the three [factors], and because it shares the same nature as such phenomena, it does not remain stable for long.
Internally, one is deluded regarding the true realm; subsequently, there are karmic conditions and the moisture of afflictions, whereby that which is produced arises.
Furthermore, because it quickly fades away and does not remain stable, it is said to "not endure for long.

Like a mirage, it is by nature flickering and turbulent; because it gives rise to transformations of immeasurable kinds of marks, it causes one to turn erroneously toward the object of perception; therefore, it is produced from the boiling waters of afflictions and craving.
It is like a springtime mirage that appears from afar to be water; many deer, tormented by heat and thirst, rush toward it.
This perception of water where there is no water is called the arising of craving.
All conditioned bodies, which arise from the various afflictions and craving, are likewise so.
As for the plantain tree, its core is not solid or substantial, and its branches and leaves, though vast, quickly wither and decay.

It is like a person with clear vision who, carrying a sharp knife, enters a forest, takes a straight plantain stalk, and cuts away its roots, branches, and leaves; finding nothing at all, how much less could there be any core?

Regarding "like an illusory phenomenon": it is, for example, like a conjurer standing at a crossroads who creates four kinds of illusory transformations; these are not at all real, because they arise from inversion.
Sūtra: "This body is like a dream... up to: it does not abide for even a single moment. Commentary:
Below are five distinct metaphors.
"Like a dream" means that what is seen in a dream is not real, because it is a false vision.
Since the body is produced by karma, karma is its essential nature, for the body is like a shadow.
The echoes in a deep valley are not substantially existent at all; these sounds belong to the causes and conditions of their original point of origin.
This body is likewise: it belongs to its original causes and conditions, and does not exist separately from them now.
They are like clouds and like lightning, as can be understood from the text.

However, while the eight similes in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* rely on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the nine similes in the *Prajñāpāramitā* [rely on it], these ten similes here show that the dependent nature is unreal, and thus constitutes emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because their meanings differ, each [text] relies on a single gate and cannot be harmonized.
The Sūtra states: "This body has no master; the four great elements constitute its home.
The Commentary says:
The fourth contemplation below concerns lack of self-mastery.
It consists of nine phrases in total: the first six phrases directly reveal that because of emptiness there is no self;
the final three phrases further reveal that because there is no self there is emptiness.
This is the first [point].
"Master" (*prabhu*) is the general name; the following four are specific names; and the final phrase generally reveals the absence of self (*anātman*).
"Master" refers to a sovereign controller, as it is the general designation for "self."
The earth has no permanent ruler; therefore, it is used as a metaphor.
I am sovereign because I depend upon the three periods of time, for sentient beings have existed from the past until the present.
"Life-principle" (*jīva*) refers to the fact that one's present lifespan can still be sustained.

"Person" (*pudgala*)—which here means "one who repeatedly undergoes rebirth"—so called because they repeatedly transmigrate through the five destinies, taking up future existences from this present moment onward.

Ordinary people and non-Buddhists falsely cling to a self that is either identical with or distinct from the three periods of time; now, taking the four great elements and space as metaphors, it is shown that their essence is entirely non-existent.
The aggregate body takes the four great elements as its abode; being a product of provisional combination, it has never been real from the beginning, and therefore possesses no self.
The self must be eternally unitary because it does not depend on anything else; however, the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and bases are not eternally unitary.
The five phrases in the older sūtra do not include this "person" (pudgala), nor do they follow the correct sequence.
These four [aspects] distinguish the self, in accordance with Vasubandhu’s *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The Sūtra says: "This body is empty... up to being driven by the power of wind.
The commentary says:
The final three phrases indicate that because there is no self, they are empty.
Since one enters into reality by means of either of these two aspects, they are empty and without substantiality, as they are free from both the self and what belongs to the self.
Because it is known, there is no self; because there is no self, it is empty.
Furthermore, there is no other cause capable of producing the body; it exists only because it is moved by the winds.
Because there is no "mine" and no "what belongs to me," it is empty.
If these were "mine," they would necessarily have been created by me;
however, through that practice of emptiness, both "I" and "mine" are emptied.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, 'I' and 'mine' do not exist; therefore, they are established as empty."
Sūtra: "This body is impure... it will inevitably return to destruction.
Commentary: This is the lower contemplation on what is loathsome and defiling.
There are seven points in total, of which two are presented here.
Regarding impurity, there are five types:
first, impurity of the seed, which is summoned by karmic retribution and formed from the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood.
Second is impurity of the dwelling place, because it is the locus of dependence within the mother’s womb between the receptacle for undigested food and the receptacle for digested food.
Third is impurity of intrinsic nature, because it is composed of the collection of thirty-six substances.
Fourth is universal impurity, because the nine orifices constantly discharge foul and filthy substances.
Fifth is ultimate impurity, because after the destruction of the body, it becomes excrement, ash, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that [the body] is filled with impurity and foulness; though one may repeatedly apply various fragrant ointments and bathe, it will ultimately return to impurity and stench.
This body is empty and fragile—who is not impure?
Impure things are necessarily deceptive, for they inevitably return to extinction.
The Sūtra says: "This body is full of afflictions and is oppressed by that which reaches it.
The Commentary states:
Regarding these two phrases:
"having many ailments" means having many diseases.

As for the "four hundred and four diseases," when one of the four great elements is disturbed, one hundred and one diseases arise; because all four great elements can be disturbed, there are thus [four hundred and] four such diseases.
The "one" is the fundamental basis, and that which arises from it constitutes the "hundred. This refers to the total number, as the upper limit reaches one hundred while the lower limit is one.

Alternatively, because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise as the resultant body induced by the causes of the ten paths of unwholesome action (*akuśala-karmapatha*), each [element] thus becomes a hundred.

Regarding the ten paths of unwholesome karma for each [of the four elements]: this is because they result in a body adorned with a hundred merits being overturned. These ten paths of unwholesome karma consist of:

(1) committing them oneself; (2) instructing others to commit them; (3) praising those who perform difficult acts; (4) rejoicing in their performance; (5) performing them to a small degree; (6) performing them to a great degree; (7) performing them in their entirety; (8) performing them for a short time; (9) performing them for a long time; and (10) performing them throughout one's entire life. Consequently, when the fruit is obtained, there arise these four great elements, as well as one hundred diseases each produced by the four great elements; together, they are collectively termed the "four hundred and four diseases."
"Like water falling down a flight of steps" refers to wells in the Western Regions; in ancient times, people bored such wells alongside paths as a shortcut, and this shortcut was called "falling.
A "flight of steps" (ji) refers to a stairway, with wooden planks serving as treads.
Furthermore, when one handles a rope or enters and exits a pavilion to fetch water, over the long course of years, it naturally becomes worn out and rotten; the body is also like this.
Or, "jie" may refer to a cord or rope; after a long time it naturally decays, and the body is also like this.
The old translation says "the well of Mount Qiu," but its meaning is difficult to comprehend.
The Sūtra states: "This body has no fixed nature... until it is composed of common aggregations.
The commentary says:
This consists of three points:
there is no fixed or permanent master, and one must inevitably die;
afflictions are like hostile bandits, and the four great elements are like venomous snakes, filling the entire body.

Just as withered grass piled up is called an "empty village," so too is the collection of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus)—the body—empty and devoid of reality; the meaning is likewise.
There are also slight differences in the older versions, which the wise should understand.
Sūtra: "O virtuous ones, you should give rise to joy.
Commentary: The following section exhorts [them] to seek [the Dharma].
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the general exhortation;
second, from "Why is that? onwards, the exhortation by way of demonstrating the characteristics.
"O virtuous ones, such are the merits of the Tathāgata’s body. This is the initial passage of the subsequent conclusion and exhortation.
It serves to conclude the preceding section while generating the following one, as it marks the characteristics of the exhortation.
Sūtra: Why is this so? The commentary states:
The following section demonstrates the exhortation through a sequence of first posing a question and subsequently providing the explanation.
This is the interrogative statement.
For what reason does one weary of such a body and rejoice in the body of a Tathāgata?
The Sūtra says: "The body of a Tathāgata... [is] that which is collectively accumulated."
The commentary states:
The following displays the characteristics.
There are three parts:
First, the characteristics of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) are shown; subsequently, the characteristics of the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) and Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) are shown.
This is the initial passage.

The Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas are formed by the collective integration of the nature of true suchness (tathatā) and myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; their manifestation and concealment are difficult to comprehend.
However, it may be stated collectively; thus it is said that "immeasurable wholesome dharmas are accomplished.
Sūtra: From the cultivation of the immeasurable up to that which is produced from wisdom.
Commentary:
The following passage reveals the merits of the two bodies: the retribution body (*vipākakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All Buddhas emerge from this sutra; all Tathāgatas are born from this sutra," because the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is thereby manifested.
The true virtues of the *saṃbhogakāya* and the manifestations of the *nirmāṇakāya* differ in their reality and their provisional nature, yet they are not distinct in their cause.
The former refers to the cause for the general virtues, while the latter refers to the causes for the specific virtues.
This is the general cause for all virtues.

Since the myriad virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are subsumed within merit and wisdom, the merits of the Buddha’s body are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); the causes explained hereafter are likewise entirely untainted.
Sūtra: "It is produced from having cultivated immeasurable supreme knowledge and vision.
Commentary:
The following section reveals the causes for its specific qualities, consisting of fifteen phrases.
Among these, one cause arises from the five aggregates:
first, the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), which has all untainted ethical discipline as its nature;
second, the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), which has all untainted meditative concentration as its nature.
The aggregate of the three types of wisdom has, as its nature, all untainted wisdom that takes conditioned phenomena as its object.
The aggregate of liberation has, as its nature, all untainted resolve (*adhimokṣa*).

The fifth is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*), which has as its nature the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that takes all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object and brings about liberation.
These five are established specifically as aggregates because they are preeminent and because they constitute a vast accumulation.
The old name for the Hīnayāna is the fivefold dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*).
According to the Sūtra, from the cultivation of compassion up to the arising of the wisdom of the power of vows,
it is praised as follows:
This consists of two sections.
The first four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are the Buddha’s actual contemplation;
the subsequent ten perfections (*pāramitā*) follow.
Subduing and tranquility consist solely of pure ethical discipline; meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, and meditative attainments consist solely of meditative absorption.
The remaining [factors] are as their respective names imply, for they have already been explained previously.
Sūtra: From the cultivation of all [virtues] up to the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, it arises.
Commentary:
This consists of five phrases.

Regarding that which arises from the cultivation of all *pāramitās*: the two benefits cultivated by Bodhisattvas are practiced such that they enable all practitioners to reach the other shore; thus, they are all termed *pāramitās*.
Because it is preeminent among the sixteen [perfections], it alone receives that name.
Now, to clarify its universal meaning, all other myriad practices are likewise called "reaching the other shore" (pāramitā).
Formerly, this was translated as "expedient means" (upāya).
Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the meaning of the six supernormal powers as skillful means has already been briefly analyzed in the section on "Majestic Power" (*prabhāva*).

As for the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*): first, the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-vidyā*); second, the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna-vidyā*); and third, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna-vidyā*). These constitute the three knowledges.

Because it eliminates and destroys obstacles, its wondrous function is difficult to fathom and its activity is vast and extensive; thus, it is established with the general name "pervasion" (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, because it removes ignorance regarding the three time periods and illuminates what is deep and distant, it is additionally established as "clarity" (*vidyā*).
The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), as well as calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) and concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*), are all as previously explained.
The Sūtra states: "From the cultivation of the ten powers (*daśabala*) up to the arising of wholesome dharmas.
The Commentary says:
This consists of four propositions.
The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities are all as previously explained.
They are so designated because the Noble Path is capable of severing evil and accumulating goodness.
Sūtra: From the cultivation of the truth of reality up to the arising of pure karma.
Commentary:
This consists of three phrases.
It arises from truthfulness, because it is produced by realizing the principle of the true reality,
or by practicing truthful conduct, or by speaking truthful words.
It arises from heedfulness, because it is originated by the prevention of evil and the cultivation of goodness.
Born of pure karma, because it arises from the extensive cultivation of the three kinds of joy.
Sūtra: "O noble ones... [up to] ...arouse the mind to seek realization.
Commentary:
The conclusion of the lower section consists of two parts:
first, an exhortation to realize the fruit; second, a joyful cultivation of the cause.

Alternatively, one may first be exhorted to realize the Buddha’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and later exhorted to cultivate the causes for the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This refers to the initial passage.
In all cases, one should resolve to seek the realization of the future fruit; or, if [the fruit] cannot arise through principle alone, one simply seeks its realization and attainment.
The original text contains only one [instance], lacking these two distinctions.
Sūtra: "If you wish to attain the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*...
Commentary: [As follows:]
This is the cause for encouraging practice.
"Cause" refers to the bodhicitta; alternatively, it refers to the cause for encouraging practice toward the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.
The cause for the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* is precisely the bodhicitta.

If one wishes to sever the diseases of afflictions and karma of all sentient beings within this body, and thereby eliminate the ailments caused by the impairment and conflict of the four great elements, one should resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The mind of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhicitta*), because it is the cause for the benefit of both self and others.
Attaining the Buddha-body is for one's own benefit; curing the illnesses of others is for the benefit of others.
Sūtra: This is the stainless Vimalakīrti’s arrival at the mind of perfect enlightenment.
The commentary states:
The following section is the third, clarifying the benefits.
Chapter 3: The Śrāvaka (Versions 3 and 4). These two subsequent chapters separately recount the former provisional teachings.
There are two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*):
first, skillfully transforming *śrāvakas*; second, skillfully transforming *bodhisattvas*.
Through skillful means he manifested illness, hoping that by inquiring after him, sentient beings would be saved.

The Buddha commanded the śrāvakas to console the Mahāsattva, but they all declined, saying that while they were formerly humbled by this Great Man, they now lack the capacity to address such matters; thus, this is called the "Chapter on the Śrāvakas."
Formerly it was called the "Chapter on Disciples.
Because his physical form resembled that of a Buddha, he alone received that title.

The Buddha knew that the consciousness of the śrāvakas was not that of a true son of the Buddha; thus, He manifested his high virtue and bestowed this name upon him, desiring to cause those of the two vehicles to practice discernment through acceptance and rejection.
In the sutra, Vimalakīrti arrives and questions me regarding my ignorance.
The commentary states:

This chapter consists of two parts; first, the skillful expedient mind conceives the wish for the Buddha to bestow his compassion; second, the Great Sage, out of pity and kindness, specifically asks [the Bodhisattvas] to go [to inquire after him].
This is the first passage.
"To lie down" means to sleep;
"suddenly" refers to the cause.
He manifested lying amidst perilous creepers in order to summon [Mañjuśrī] to inquire after his illness.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for him...
Commentary: It says:
The Great Sage, out of compassion, specifically requested that [the interlocutor] go to inquire.
This major section has three parts:
first, the intent behind the request to inquire;...
Next, he commissioned ten virtuous men, all of whom declined on the grounds that they were unfit for the task;
subsequently, he summoned the śrāvakas by category, and all declined without dispersing.
This is the first passage.
The ten great śrāvakas may be briefly categorized into five pairs: those who internally pacify body and mind while externally manifesting eloquence and principle;

those who specifically relieve poverty and suffering while equally manifesting compassion; those who instruct beginners while teaching and perfecting those already learned; those who adapt to circumstances to guide the virtuous while causing others to repent and cease transgressions; and those who praise the life of renunciation while establishing rules for seeking alms and receiving service.
They were paired accordingly; had they remained silent, their paths would have diverged and their provisional methods would have become distinct.
Consequently, the ten sages were silenced and divided into five pairs.
The Sūtra records that [the Buddha] addressed Śāriputra and inquired after his health.
The commentary states:
"The ten virtuous ones who were dispatched with the imperial decree all found their words inadequate."
Every sentence has two components:
first, the imperative; second, the declarative.
This is an imperative.
Sūtra: Śāriputra went to visit him and inquire after his illness.
Commentary: This refers to the "lower harmony."
Each section contains three parts:

first, a general statement that the Way has been exhausted; second, a specific demonstration that the principle has reached its limit; and third, a concluding response that humbles oneself with humble words to request withdrawal.
This is the first section.
Although Śāriputra’s body and mind were tranquil, he could not transcend his physical form within the three realms.
By removing clamor to enter stillness, he was unable to function while remaining in that very tranquility.
For this reason, he was constrained by circumstances and replied that he was incapable.
Sūtra: Why is this so? Commentary:
This section below reveals the ultimate exhaustion of principle.
Each passage contains two parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the explanation.
This is the inquiry.
Sūtra: "Recalling me, [he went] as far as sitting beneath the tree of meditation.
Commentary: The following clarifies the limits of the expression.
Each passage consists of two parts:
first, the presentation of one's own account; second, the citation of another’s words.
This is the initial passage.
If one reads "yàn" with the *wūjiān* (烏間) tone, it means silence.
Now, it is read as "yàn" with the *wūjiàn* (烏見) tone, meaning peace.

Upon entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because the arising of the six contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-ṣaḍvijñāna*) inevitably involves mental toil, and out of weariness toward them, they are now rendered non-functional.
Since there are already seven untainted [factors], only six are mentioned here.
For those of the two vehicles, when they enter the state of the mind of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), they cause the mind and its mental factors to become increasingly subtle and minute.

At the time of the subtle mind, the function of the seeds perfumed [by it] which causes the six consciousnesses not to operate is precisely what is called the "attainment of cessation" (nirodhasamāpatti).
This is established based on seeds, as explained in another chapter.

Alternatively, "one who sits in meditation" refers to one who has entered the meditative absorption of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), thereby bringing body and mind to a state of tranquil stillness;
it does not refer to the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). At that time, Vimalakīrti arrived and spoke these words.
The commentary states:
The following reveals the words of others.
Each passage contains two parts.
First, the preliminary exposition of the ultimate path; second, the formal presentation of the discourse.
This is the first section.
Although his stainless virtue and reputation were lofty, his physical form conformed to that of an ordinary person.
The path of the śrāvaka occupies an inferior station, yet its outward appearance resembles that of a Tathāgata; thus, it transforms sentient beings by conforming to their various types.

When [the Emperor] came in person to pay homage with his head bowed, Kumārajīva was reduced to silence before the Lord of Yao, and being stained by the dust of desire, he entered secular society as a guest of an elder and joined the monastic community wearing the robes of a śrāmaṇera. Unable to compel those of high virtue to bend and perform the prostration of a subordinate toward the ranks of monks, he consequently excised the protocols for visitors and omitted entirely any mention of bowing the head.
According to the Sanskrit original, all [these sections] are present.
In this sutra, however, it begins with Śāriputra and concludes with "sitting in meditation.
The commentary states:
Now the formal argument is presented in three parts:
first, a general refutation; second, a specific refutation; and third, a concluding refutation.
This is a general negation.
"Only" (*wei*) is a term used for respectful assent.
"Tranquil" (*yan*) carries the meaning of peaceful stillness.

The meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) of the two vehicles stills the mind of toil and anxiety; it severs the攀缘攀想 (clinging thoughts) within the field of the emotions and settles the physical body in forests and wilds—this is called "seated in tranquility" (*yansuo*).
Since it is not the tranquil concentration of the Mahāyāna, it is rejected in its entirety;
yet, as this is not a total rejection, it is said that it is "not necessarily" so.
Sūtra: Now, as for "sitting in quietude," up to this point is what constitutes sitting in quietude.
The commentary states:
The following section refutes [the opponent's] position.
There are six principles; this is the refutation of the first principle.
Now, as for "sitting in quietude" (*yansuo*), this term summarizes the essence of "quietude.
Regarding the meaning of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the "Principles of Reasoning" (*Yingli yi*) states:
there are four dharma-gates: first, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); second, consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*); third, signlessness (*animitta*); and fourth, suchness (*tathatā*).
The principles of the latter three dharma-gates can all be understood;
however, the gate of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is the most difficult.
Hereafter, the explanation will focus specifically on the gate of dependent origination.
The remaining three [points] are easy to understand and thus will not be elaborated upon further.
When a śrāvaka sits in meditative seclusion, he does not manifest a mind that pertains to the triple world.
In the Tathāgata’s extinction samādhi, even the contaminated body ceases; therefore, he relinquishes impermanent form and attains eternal form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
To enter into tranquil concentration is what is called true sitting in meditation.
When the Buddha teaches beginners, he says that one should only extinguish the mind; if the physical form is not yet dissolved, it is not true tranquil concentration.
Because it is half-true and half-false, it is said that it is not necessarily so.
Regarding the essential meaning of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*, the principle of emptiness states:

the two vehicles do not realize that the characteristics of form and mind are empty; therefore, when they conceal their bodies in the forest or enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), although they intend to hide and extinguish themselves, they instead become manifest.

The Great Being knows that form and mind are themselves emptiness; because he does not necessarily require the establishment of quiescence, he does not manifest body or mind within the three realms—this is called "sitting in meditation.
As the Sūtra says: "Not arising from the samādhi of cessation until this is achieved is what constitutes sitting in meditation."
The commentary says:
This is the second "non-.
Regarding the principle of emptiness, Master Kongyun said:
The followers of the Two Vehicles have limited views, dividing stillness and function into two; thus, they cease activity to enter stillness, which is called "sitting in meditation" (*yànzuò*).

The Great Being (Bodhisattva), however, widely propagates the truth by arising from stillness into function; thus, he can extinguish body and mind within tranquil concentration, yet give rise to wondrous function within every deportment.
The *Yingliyi* (Meaning of Correspondence to Principle) states:

When those of the two vehicles enter quiescence, their preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) is subtle; they pacify both body and mind and lack the capacity for action. Thus, they function without being quiescent, and are quiescent without functioning.

When a Bodhisattva enters cessation, their skillful means and wisdom are powerful; they first strike the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) to manifest majestic deportment and give rise to the wondrous function of benefiting sentient beings, only after which do the six consciousnesses enter the meditative absorption of cessation.

Externally manifesting through body and speech, one may temporarily appear to possess a mind; yet internally ceasing all攀緣 (pān-yuán, cognitive clinging), when one truly enters cessation, then stillness itself functions—this is called true *dhyāna* (seated meditation).
Sūtra: Not abandoning anything—this is what constitutes sitting in meditation.
Commentary: The third [position] is unreasonable.
The following passage concerning "sitting in meditation" (yànzuò) does not necessarily refer to the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
According to the principle of the meaning of emptiness:

the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are unable to regard purity as defilement; therefore, they enter into purity by extinguishing defilement, and this constitutes their sitting in meditation.
The Great Being’s principle of saving both the good and the evil is such that the ultimate and conventional truths are viewed as one.
According to the meaning of the *Yingli* (Correspondence to Principle):
"In the stages of the Two Vehicles, the functions of wisdom differ; when the wisdom that contemplates the ultimate manifests before them, the conventional function immediately ceases."
Conventional wisdom arises to function, while true wisdom does not operate.

Because the Bodhisattva has long cultivated skillful means and their application is perfectly harmonized, they remain inwardly tranquil within the true realm while outwardly manifesting the phenomena of ordinary beings; the characteristic of what is thus realized is the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
The dharmas of ordinary beings refer to afflictions and the like.
From the fifth bhūmi onward, correct wisdom realizes the ultimate truth, while subsequent wisdom arises regarding the conventional.

From the eighth bhūmi upward, one spontaneously observes both simultaneously; thus, one can internally cease from grasping at objects and externally manifest the dharmas of ordinary beings—this is called true *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation).
The old translation states: "Not abandoning the internal marks realized within the dharmas of the Path"; the phrasing differs, but the meaning is the same.
Sūtra: When the mind does not dwell within—this is called sitting in meditation.
The commentary states:
The fourth [position] is unreasonable.
The meaning of the principle of emptiness is as follows:

Those of the Two Vehicles perceive the nature of the mind as existing; they dwell internally within the six sense organs and externally grasp the six sense objects. To cease this, they enter into tranquil concentration (*śamatha-samādhi*).

The Bodhisattva knows that the nature of the mind is not existent and realizes that both the faculties and their objects are empty. This is called "ceasing the mind of discrimination"; therefore, by dwelling neither internally nor externally, it is called true *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation).
The *Yingliyi* (Meaning of the Correct Principle) states:

"The objects of contemplation for the two vehicles do not exceed the internal and external. 'Internal' refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and 'external' refers to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*); these twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) encompass all phenomena."
Because this mind is able to produce weariness [with existence] until reaching the stage of total exhaustion, it is called "entering meditative absorption.
Therefore, various teachings state:
"One enters the attainment of cessation by forming the perception of 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception' (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)."

When a Bodhisattva enters quiescence, they enter by contemplating only the truth of signlessness (*animitta*), not bringing about the cessation of the mind by depending on internal or external objects; this is called true sitting in meditation (*pratisaṃlayanā*).
Therefore, various teachings state:
"One enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by relying on the characteristic of the realm of signlessness."

It is further said: "To dwell in true emptiness, to cease all discursive thoughts, not to wander between the internal and external, and to be free from established signs—this is called true sitting in meditation.
The Sūtra says: "Dwelling in the thirty-seven [factors of enlightenment]... this is what constitutes sitting in meditation."
The commentary states:
The fifth [position] is unreasonable.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are called "factors" because they are the primary causes for realizing awakening.
The *Kongliyi* states:

The followers of the two vehicles are unable to transform the erroneous into the correct; therefore, they abandon the erroneous to enter the correct, which is called "sitting in meditation" (*yànzuò*).

Bodhisattvas, however, transform the erroneous into the correct; thus, while abiding in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), they do not depart from the modes of perception, which is called "true sitting in meditation."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Regarding 'views' (*dṛṣṭigata*): the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—these five types of views are what is meant by the term 'views'."
Alternatively, it is the destination to which the five views resort, namely the realms of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Because those dwelling in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) of the Two Vehicles cannot transform the evil views and realms of the non-Buddhists, it is called "detachment" (*viveka*).
When a bodhisattva dwells within the factors of the path while externally transforming the various heterodoxies, this is called "not departing" and is termed "true sitting in meditation.
The old interpretation—that one "remains unmoved amidst all views while practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment"—is incorrect; how could such a state be called true cessation?
Sūtra: Not abandoning birth and death—this is what constitutes sitting in meditation.
Commentary: The sixth [point] is unreasonable.
The *Kongliyi* states:

"The followers of the Two Vehicles cannot transform bondage into liberation; therefore, having severed their bonds, they abandon birth and death, and having realized nirvana, they abide in something."
It should be understood as follows:
although a bodhisattva, like ordinary beings, does not abandon birth and death, he is nonetheless different due to his great wisdom, and thus he is free from afflictions;
although he, like those of the two vehicles, realizes nirvana, he is nonetheless different due to his great compassion, and thus he has no fixed abode.
The followers of the two vehicles are not like this: if they abandon birth and death, they immediately sever their afflictions; if they realize nirvana, they necessarily abide therein.
Therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva is one who truly enters into quiescence.
The old [translation] states, "One enters nirvana without severing afflictions," whereas the present [text] says there are no afflictions; the reasoning here is quite contradictory.
Alternatively, one might say that because one retains delusions, one does not sever the afflictions, yet by realizing the non-abiding state, this is called entering nirvana.
Sūtra: "If one can thus [proceed], one will reach the point where it is approved by the Buddha.
Commentary:
This conclusion is incorrect.
One who possesses the aforementioned virtues and sits in meditative equipoise accords with correct principle and is approved by the Buddha, for they are fully endowed with practice.
Conversely, one who enters stillness without possessing these prior conditions is not approved by the Buddha, as this is the practice of the partial and limited vehicles.
Sūtra:
At that time, our World-Honored One went to visit him to inquire about his illness.
Praise says:
Regarding the third section here, the conclusion of the response consists of the words by which he humbly requests to withdraw.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One... [inquired] after his illness.
The Commentary states:
The following text has two parts; this is the first, the address.
In Sanskrit it is called Mahā-maudgalyāyana; here it is translated as "Great Maudgalya. As for "maudgalya," *maudga* refers to beans (*śu*).
"Shi" refers to a clan or lineage.
In ancient times, there was an immortal who constantly ate *yuán* beans; he was a descendant of that person, and thus he was named the Great Collector of Beans (*Dà Cǎishū Shì*).
The origins of this individual, as well as those of Śāriputra, Mahākāśyapa, and others, are all explained in the first volume of the *Commentary on the Maitreya’s Rebirth Above Sūtra*.
After some time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to visit him to inquire about his illness.
He praised [the Buddha] and said:
"I am unworthy to decline his invitation."
The passage contains three parts:

first, a general statement that his Way has been thwarted; second, a specific demonstration that his principles have reached their limit; and third, a concluding response in which he humbles himself and requests to withdraw.
This is the general statement that his Way has been thwarted.

Maudgalyāyana manifested the principles of words and logic externally, yet he could not internally accord with the ineffable; although he spoke of the emptiness of the self, he could not discourse on the non-existence of dharmas. For this reason, he was overcome and thus replied that he was incapable.
Sūtra: Why is this so? [It continues] up to "expounding the essential points of the Dharma.
Commentary: The following section reveals the ultimate exhaustion of principle.
The text contains two parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the exposition.
Within the exposition, there are again two sections:
This first passage first states the matter at hand and subsequently clarifies the words of another.
"Qu" (衢) means a path or way.
The roads leading in the four directions are called "four-way crossroads.
Formerly, these were referred to as "streets and alleys.
At that time, Vimalakīrti arrived and spoke these words.
The commentary states:
The following reveals the words of others.
There are two parts:
First, his position is stated; subsequently, the formal argument is presented.
This is the initial passage.
Scripture: "O Mahāmaudgalyāyana... [it] should be explained according to the Dharma."
The commentary says:
The following is the formal presentation of the argument.
This text consists of four parts:
First, a general negation;
second, a counter-interrogation;
third, a specific negation.
The fourfold "elucidation of benefit" refers to instances such as the eight hundred lay devotees (gṛhapati) generating the aspiration for enlightenment.
The older texts contain only three [points] and lack this "rebuttal by interrogation.
When it says, "It should not be as the Venerable One has stated," the intended meaning is that the reasoning in the Venerable One's exposition of the Dharma is incorrect.
"Appropriate" (dàng) means "to accord with.
To speak without acceding to principle is called "inappropriate" (bùdāng).
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (kōnglǐ):
The principle of dharmas is fundamentally empty; yet the Śrāvakas claim they exist, and thus their words are incorrect.
According to the meaning that accords with reason:
dharmas lack the two kinds of self, for their nature is beyond verbal expression.
That teaching of the Dharma exists, yet it is not apart from ineffability; therefore, it is said to be "inappropriate.
For one who teaches the Dharma does so in accordance with the Dharma.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, I asked: '...up to: is it taught in accordance with the Dharma?'"
The commentary says:
This is a refutation by means of questioning.
The Sūtra states:
He replied, "Because the past and future limits have been severed.
[The commentator] praised this, saying:
"The following [explanation] is incorrect."
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the revelation of the principle of the two kinds of selflessness;
second, from the passage beginning with "Now, as for those who preach the Dharma," the clarification of the principle of preaching the Dharma.
The beginning and middle further consist of two parts:
first, clarifying non-self;
second, concluding on non-self, as in the passage: "Since the characteristics of dharmas are thus, how can they be spoken?"
Within the clarification of selflessness, there are further two parts:
first, the clarification of the selflessness of sentient beings; second, the clarification of the selflessness of phenomena.
This [section] clarifies the selflessness of sentient beings.

The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) throughout the three periods of time are fundamentally without self; yet, by reckoning what is not-self as self, one increases this "self" like a stain, thereby defiling the original nature.
All phenomena (*dharma*) of the past are fundamentally without sentient beings (*sattva*); yet, by clinging to them as sentient beings, they become defiled like dust.
Present phenomena originally lack a "life-principle" (jīva), yet one clings to them as being a life-principle, thereby increasing birth and death.
That which currently lives and survives is termed a "life-principle.
To cling to this as truly existent is precisely to cling to the existence of real birth and death.
Alternatively, they may hold that because there is currently birth and death, there is a "life-principle" (jīva);
yet now, being free from birth and death, there is no life-principle.

They further maintain that while future phenomena lack a "person" (pudgala), there is one in the present; thus, once the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has been severed in the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), it is born within the six destinies (*ṣadgati*) in the subsequent limit (*aparānta*).
"Severance" (*cheda*) signifies the meaning of emptiness and non-existence.
Since there is ultimately no anteriority or posteriority within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), how could there be any real number of sentient beings (*sattva*)?
These four types of selflessness are consistent with the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and also accord with the fourfold [selflessness] taught in the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
The Master Kongliyi said:
"If conventional truth exists, it may have four aspects.
But since ultimate truth is empty, how can there be four?"
Therefore, when speaking of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), one should speak of the four emptinesses.
The meaning according to reason is that even within conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), these four lack reality.
Based on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), both the dependent nature (*paratantra*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) likewise lack reality.
Therefore, according to ultimate truth, one should speak of the four emptinesses (*catasraḥ śūnyatāḥ*).
When Śrāvakas preach the Dharma, they do not enumerate the four existences (*catvāro bhavāḥ*).
Now, speaking generally, because the nature of all dharmas is detached from both persons and dharmas, the four emptinesses are taught.
The ancients were mistaken; one should understand this by referring to the new [exegesis].
Sūtra: "The Dharma is eternally quiescent... up to: because it has no object of cognition."
The commentary states:
The following explains the emptiness of dharmas.
There are twenty phrases.
The principle of emptiness states:
according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) exists;
according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the nature of phenomena is entirely empty.
However, because it serves to destroy all attachments to differentiation, it is explained separately; thus, the subsequent phrase can be used to further clarify the preceding one.

Because conventional reality possesses characteristics (*nimitta*), it is not quiescent; because ultimate reality is without characteristics, it is tranquil. This is the emptiness of the objective realm.

Because the conventional has an object of perception (*ālambana*), there is greedy attachment; because the ultimate is without an object of perception, one is free from greed—this is the emptiness of that which can perceive.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these twenty phrases are divided into two parts: the first ten phrases reveal the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*tathatā*) being free from grasped objects, while the latter ten phrases reveal the emptiness of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) being free from grasped objects.
Alternatively, twenty phrases all describe *tathatā* (suchness); for *tathatā* is quiescent, as it extinguishes the ten marks;
and *tathatā* is free from greed, as it is not an object of conceptualizing mind.

Regarding the traditional statement that "dharmas are free from marks," even the mark of craving may be without hindrance. First, one is freed from the mark of the object of cognition (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*); subsequently, one is freed from the mark of the subject of cognition (*ālambaka-lakṣaṇa*). Since the mind that craves and clings to the subject of cognition lacks an objective realm, that mind itself also ceases to exist.
Sūtra: “The Dharma is without words, up to the point that it is beyond the thoughts of waves.
Commentary: Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness: because conventional existence involves speech, there are words; [but in ultimate reality, these do not exist].
Ultimate truth transcends speech; therefore, it is devoid of words and letters.
Conventional reality involves conceptual thought, which arises and surges like waves upon water; therefore, it employs metaphorical explanations.
Ultimate truth is free from conceptual thought; therefore, it is devoid of metaphorical explanations.
The *Yingliyi* (Meaning of the Appropriate Principle) states:
Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is described as "severed," it is devoid of words and letters.
Because True Suchness transcends worldly waves of thought, it is beyond metaphorical description.
The former [text] states: "Dharmas are beyond verbal expression because they are free from vitarka and vicāra," for waves, thoughts, and the like are precisely vitarka and vicāra. The Sūtra says:
"Dharmas pervade all things, reaching even to the activities of movement."
The commentary states:
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness, it is said that the conventional is not like emptiness, for its nature of existence is not pervasive;
whereas the principle of reality is empty by nature, and therefore pervades all things.
In the conventional world, there are activities such as bending and stretching; therefore, there are manifest colors, as well as indicative marks and shapes.
Since in reality there are no activities such as bending and stretching, how could there possibly be manifest characteristics, shapes, and so forth?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"True Suchness (tathatā) is like space; its nature is without obstruction, and thus it pervades all things. Furthermore, because it lacks such activities as moving, bending, or stretching, it is devoid of manifest characteristics, form, color, and so forth."
"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to manifest form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the two passages in the ancient sūtras, they differ slightly.
The first is like space; it is said that, being devoid of form and characteristics, it is able to pervade all things.
Ultimate emptiness is said to be free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Conceptual proliferation refers to manifest characteristics and formal shapes.
Ultimate emptiness is so called because it is devoid of formations (*saṃskāra*) and the like.
Sūtra: “Because phenomena are devoid of ‘mine’ and because they transcend mind and consciousness. Commentary:
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness: because worldly attachment holds that there is a self and what belongs to a self, phenomena are said to possess a self and what belongs to a self.
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no object of attachment; therefore, phenomena (*dharma*) have no "mine" (*mamakāra*).
In the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), there is mind and consciousness, and phenomena are established as objects of cognition;
in the ultimate, there is no mind or consciousness, and thus phenomena are not objects of cognition.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Suchness (*tathatā*) is not the self; therefore, it is free from what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).
Thus, various treatises say:"
The *tathatā* (suchness) that is without appropriation is not the basis for the grasping of self-clinging and the like.
Suchness is not an object of comprehension, because it is free from the domain of mind and consciousness, and because it transcends the conceptualization of mind and consciousness.
Reality is not an object, or rather, there is no capacity to cognize it, because it is apart from mind and consciousness.
The Sūtra says: "Dharmas have no counterpart, up to: they do not abide within conditions.
The Commentary states:
The principle of emptiness states that conventional reality is dependent and phenomena possess comparison;
true reality is non-dependent, and therefore possesses no comparison.
Within conventional reality, there are conditions, and thus it belongs to causes, because it is obtained through causes.
Because there are no conditions within reality (*tathatā*), it does not belong to causes; for all phenomena produced by causes and conditions are said to be empty.
The meaning that accords with principle states:
the wondrousness of *tathatā* is peerless, as there is nothing else that can exist in relation to it.
Suchness does not belong to causes; because it is not obtained through conditions and is not produced by causes, it is said that its name does not reside in conditions.
As the Sūtra says: "The Dharma is identical to the Dharma-realm, reaching to the point of non-following."
The commentary states:
Regarding the principle of emptiness, it is said that conventional truth involves the adherence to the existence of phenomena, which is not the same as the dharma-realm;
whereas within ultimate truth, all things equally enter the true dharma-realm, and thus, being identical to the dharma-realm, all are empty.
The conventional has that which it follows; it does not follow suchness because it follows existence.
The ultimate truth has nothing to follow because it does not follow existence; both, however, follow the emptiness of suchness.
The *Yingliyi* (Meaning of the Correct Principle) states:

The following ten phrases clarify that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is empty of the grasped object, and further demonstrate that the dependent is subsumed and returned to suchness (*tathatā*).

Because the nature of the dependent is identical to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it subsumes characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) back into the nature (*svabhāva*) and enters the dharma-realm; thus, it differs from the falsely existent conceptualizations of the grasped.
The ancients said, "Because it enters into all phenomena. The Dharma-realm is the Dharma;
it demonstrates conformity with Suchness (*tathatā*), for there is no Suchness to be grasped that one could conform to.
The Sūtra says: "The Dharma abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)... because it does not rely on the six objects of cognition."
The commentary states:
That which moves is disordered movement.
The ultimate limit of reality is called the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*); it has the meaning of being an object of focus that is free from error.
The principle of emptiness states:
the conventional is subject to movement and thus does not abide in the limit of reality;
the ultimate is devoid of movement and therefore abides in the limit of reality.
The conventional depends upon the six objects, and therefore the phenomena are subject to fluctuation;
True Suchness does not depend upon the six, and therefore it is without fluctuation.
That which fluctuates can be destroyed, can be ruined, and can be overturned.
The *Yingli yi* (Meaning of the Appropriate Principle) states:
"Abiding in the dependent nature within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it follows along with that limit of reality and is ultimately unmoving.
As for the ancient saying, "Unmoved by any extremes," it means that the various extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are unable to move it.
The dependent nature is likewise immovable, for it conforms to suchness and does not rely upon the six sense objects.
Sūtra: "Because phenomena have no coming or going, nor increase or decrease, they are beyond conceptualization."
The commentary states:
Regarding the principle of emptiness, it is said that in the conventional there is a place of abiding, with coming and going;
yet in the ultimate truth there is no abiding—whither could one go, and from where could one come?

Because worldly beings possess thoughts of augmentation, they do not accord with emptiness; because they cling to things as being existent, and because they possess thoughts of diminution, they do not follow signlessness or correspond to wishlessness, for they negate [existence] by treating it as non-existent.

Because there is no superimposition within reality (*tathatā*), it accords with the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and thus lacks any diminution; it conforms to signlessness (*animitta*) and corresponds to wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
According to the meaning of the principle:
that which is dependent (*paratantra*) follows reality and likewise has neither coming nor going, for it has no place of abiding.
The "departed" refers to the past and the "coming" refers to the future; because there is no present abiding, there is consequently no departing or coming.
If there were something that abided, then departing and coming would depend upon it, and one would not accord with signlessness (*animitta*) or respond to wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Because one accords with suchness (*tathatā*), free from thoughts of increase or decrease, one is thus able to conform to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), follow signlessness, and respond to wishlessness.

The ancients said, "The Dharma is without increase or decrease," which at first glance seems like a separate statement; however, according to this new text, it serves to explain the preceding meaning.
The phrase from the ancients, "The Dharma is free from the beautiful and the ugly," is absent in the new text; I do not know why this was added outside of the original principle.
Sūtra: Because the Dharma is without taking or rejecting, it reaches the path of body and mind. Commentary:

Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness: in the conventional sense, because there is arising, there is that which can be taken up; because there is cessation, there is that which can be rejected.
In ultimate reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing; what, then, is there to grasp or to abandon?
"The Way" (Dharma) signifies the principle of universal penetration; the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) constitute the Way.
In the conventional sense, the six faculties serve as the "grasping storehouse," and thus the phenomena of the six objects become the "objectified storehouse."
The True is not that which is stored within the six sense organs; therefore, the Dharma has no storehouse of grasping, for it transcends the path of the six sense organs.
The meaning according to principle states:
the dependent nature conforms to the True, being without grasping or abandoning, as it is free from arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, there is no "appropriating store" (*upādānagarbha*); it transcends the six sense faculties because it is not an object of craving, yet it is not that which is not an appropriating store.

The ancients said, "Dharmas are without arising or ceasing. While the first phrase can establish the non-existence of dharmas, the term "that to which they return" carries the meaning of an appropriating store, yet its underlying reason is not explained.
Sūtra: "The Dharma has no high or low, up to the point of ultimate cessation.
Commentary:

Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): "movement and transformation" refers to the sense of mutual dependence; "proliferation" (*prapañca*) refers to false conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The conventional is not without movement, and phenomena have degrees of high and low;
in the ultimate truth there is no shifting or turning, so what high or low could there be?
Because conceptual proliferation is not severed within the conventional, this is the domain of the discriminating mind.
Within reality (*tattva*), all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is ultimately severed; therefore, it is free from the sphere of all discursive discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The meaning according to principle is as follows:
the dependent nature (*paratantra*) conforms to reality (*tathatā*); being neither high nor low, it abides in immovability.
It is also free from all that is traversed by conceptualization, because conceptual proliferation has been utterly severed.
The ancient saying, "The Dharma is free from all modes of contemplative practice," refers here to what is traversed by conceptualization.
Discrimination refers to the process of contemplative practice.

Within the meaning that accords with principle, these twenty phrases all describe the dharmas of *tathatā* (suchness) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); they do not accord with what is grasped by the discriminating mind, nor do they accord with their verbalized nature—all of which are said to be non-existent. It is not that the essence of *tathatā* itself becomes empty.
For now, let us follow the explanation according to the most eminent meaning; this does not contradict reason.
These twenty phrases should be understood as ten pairs.
I have briefly concluded here for fear that a detailed examination of each one would result in excessive textual prolixity.
Sūtra: "Only Mahāmaudgalyāyana... how could it be said [otherwise]? Commentary:
This concludes the section on non-self (*anātman*).
The Meaning of Emptiness (Kong-ri) says:
"In the context of the supreme truth, the dharma-nature is empty in this manner; how could it be as it is expressed by words?
The Meaning of Accordance with Principle (Eung-ri) says:
Although the essence of phenomena exists, it does not exist with the intrinsic nature as it is conceptually differentiated or as it is expressed in speech; how, then, can it be described?
The Sūtra states: "One who teaches the Dharma is said to fall into the extremes of superimposition and denial."
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the principles of preaching the Dharma.
Within this, there are further two parts:
First, there is a general discussion on the principles of listening;
subsequently, from the passage beginning with "Venerable Maudgalyāyana," there is an exhortation to speak according to the Dharma.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness:
If that which is ultimately empty in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is said to exist for the sake of teaching and listening, this is termed "superimposition" (*samāropa*).
If that which inherently exists in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is said to be non-empty, it becomes "denial" (*apavāda*).
Alternatively, failing to accord with the true intrinsic nature (*dharmasvabhāva*) of phenomena as a whole is termed "augmentation or diminution" (*samāropa-apavāda*).
The meaning that accords with reason is as follows:
conceptualizing apart from phenomena and giving rise to verbal expression is termed "augmentation" (*samāropa*), because it is like adding something extraneous to a phenomenon.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Both the signifier and the signified lack intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
They function solely by relying on superimposition (*samāropa*) and resemblance.
"Resemblance" refers to superimposition; it is not a truly existent characteristic.
Because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are not objects for either conceptual cognition or its verbal designations.
To say that there is no essence of phenomena is called "denigration" (*apavāda*), because it negates their existence.
Alternatively, it refers to increasing what is conceptually grasped and diminishing the non-dual nature.
The old translation states, "without speaking, without showing, without hearing, and without attaining," but this is not correct, as these specific words do not appear [in the source].
Sūtra: "If, in a location, there is that which reaches all cognitions."
The commentary states:
This establishes the correct principle.
If one realizes the wisdom of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), one realizes that the essence of phenomena is without increase or decrease; thus, all phenomena are ultimately ineffable.

The ancients said, "There is no speaking and no showing. If the listener possesses wisdom, they realize and accord with the essence of the Dharma as being neither increasing nor decreasing; since it cannot even be heard, what is there to be discerned? How, then, can one say, "I have understood"?
In this regard, there is a doubt:
if both the speaker of the Dharma and the listener undergo increase or decrease, how does the Buddha speak,
and how do the great Bodhisattvas listen?
Therefore, the scripture explains this clearly:
"Venerable Maudgalyāyana, only when [the time] arrives may you preach the Dharma.
The commentary states:
The following exhorts one to speak according to the Dharma.
First, it resolves doubts and demonstrates the characteristics of the teaching; subsequently, it exhorts one to practice accordingly.

For example, it is like a master illusionist who, for the sake of illusory beings, proclaims all dharmas to illusory listeners using illusory persons and illusory names. These dharmas are entirely devoid of even the slightest reality; they serve merely as a raft-like metaphor, and thus they are free from the extremes of exaggeration and depreciation.
Therefore, when the Buddha teaches the Dharma, the Bodhisattvas are able to hear it; they do not give rise to attachment by discriminating the intrinsic nature of what is taught.
Sūtra: "O good son, you should know that [this leads] to the manifestation of great compassion."
The commentary states:
The following exhortation to practice consists of eight matters.
Among these, there are three:
First, knowing the faculties and roots of sentient beings;
second, wisdom that penetrates all phenomena without obstruction—
where "obstruction" (guà) means hindrance and "impediment" (ài) means confinement.
The three great compassions manifest.
The Sūtra states that one should teach the Mahāyāna up to the point of expounding the Dharma.
The Commentary says:
This consists of five points:
four praise the Mahāyāna,
and the fifth is mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Sixth is the purity of one’s own intention, due to profound faith and resolute conviction.
Seventh is skillfulness in the Dharma and its expression: skillfulness in the Dharma is the absence of obstruction regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*);
skillfulness in expression is the absence of obstruction regarding language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).
Alternatively, "dharma-words" refers to the words used for expounding the Dharma, characterized by unimpeded eloquence.
The eighth [quality] is that one is able to perpetuate and honor the seeds of the Triple Gem.
One should expound the Dharma only when endowed with these eight qualities.
Because śrāvakas lack these eight qualities, they should not preach the Dharma.
By reversing each of these points, the meaning becomes clear.
The older translations list six qualities, omitting "purity of intention" and "skillfulness in dharma and phrasing."
Sūtra: From the time the World-Honored One attained the mind of Perfect Enlightenment, it was praised as:
the fourth presentation of benefit.
At that time of interrogation, the assembly gained great benefit.
After some time had passed, our World-Honored One went to visit him to inquire about his illness.
He praised [the situation], saying:
This is the third point, concluding the response by requesting to withdraw due to one’s humble demeanor.
Because I did not respond at that time, it is called "silence.
Being unable to recognize or understand the explanation thus spoken is termed "lack of discernment."
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One went to inquire after his illness.
He praised him, saying:
"From this point downward, the third [section] commands Mahākāśyapa."
The text also has two parts:
first, the command; second, the response.
This is the initial command.
Mahākāśyapa is translated here as "Great Drinker of Light.
In ancient times there was a rishi whose body and skin were golden in color, and who was able to drink in the light of the sun and moon; Kāśyapa is of that lineage.
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa’s body was also golden in radiance, eclipsing the light of the sun and moon; thus he was named "The Eclipsing Radiance" (Pītabhāsa).
The account of these causes and conditions is as found in the *Maitreya-vyākhyā*.
